idiom_name: per-store module with an opaque handle and operation functions (sqlite3-style)
implementation_notes: C has no interfaces, so the DAO is a hand-written boundary: expose one header per aggregate whose functions take an opaque handle (a struct defined only in the .c file, exactly as SQLite hides its connection behind sqlite3 and its compiled statements behind sqlite3_stmt) and keep every SQL string and driver call inside that translation unit. Data crosses the boundary in caller-supplied structs, never as a sqlite3_stmt, and driver result codes such as SQLITE_CONSTRAINT are mapped to the module's own status enum before returning. When more than one store must be swappable at run time, add a struct of function pointers - one slot per operation - plus a constructor that returns it; with a single store the plain module is simpler and already isolates the quirk.
pitfalls: Nothing in the C type system enforces the boundary: a client can still include the driver header and bypass the DAO, so the isolation holds by convention, header discipline and review, not by the compiler.
Every function needs its ownership contract documented: who closes the handle, who owns the character data copied into the transfer struct, and what state *out is left in when the call fails.
Returning raw driver codes couples callers to the store; translate SQLITE_* and similar values into the module's status enum inside the implementation.
